STATEMENT OF PARTNERSHIP AUTHORITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan & Lee Consulting · Jordan T. Reyes

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — STATEMENT OF PARTNERSHIP AUTHORITY INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes a specific public filing California law makes available to a general partnership: a statement of partnership authority filed with the Secretary of State under Corporations Code section 16303, part of the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 (Corp. Code §§ 16100 et seq.). A statement of partnership authority is a document a partnership may (not must) file to publicly identify its partners or an authorized agent, to name the partners authorized to transfer real property held in the partnership's name, and optionally to state other grants or limits on individual partners' authority to act for Morgan & Lee Consulting. This sheet states what the statute itself provides about that filing — its required content, its legal effect on partners' authority as to third parties, the related statement of denial, and the general filing mechanics that apply to statements under this chapter. It does not draft or file a statement of partnership authority for Morgan & Lee Consulting, does not determine whether Morgan & Lee Consulting should file one, and does not address the separate topics covered elsewhere in this corpus: the partnership agreement governing the partners' own relationship (General Partnership Agreement document) or the dissolution and winding-up of a general partnership (General Partnership Dissolution and Winding-Up — Information Sheet).

THE DEFAULT RULE ABSENT A FILED STATEMENT: EACH PARTNER IS AN AGENT OF THE PARTNERSHIP
Independently of whether Morgan & Lee Consulting ever files a statement of partnership authority, California's Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 already makes each partner an agent of the partnership for the purpose of its business. An act of a partner — including executing an instrument in the partnership's name — that apparently carries on the partnership's business, or business of the kind the partnership carries on, in the ordinary course binds the partnership, unless the partner in fact lacked authority and the other party knew or had been notified of that lack of authority. An act that is not apparently within the ordinary course, by contrast, binds the partnership only if the other partners actually authorized it. A filed statement of partnership authority does not replace this default agency rule; the statute frames the default rule itself as operating "subject to the effect of a statement of partnership authority" where one has been filed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Each partner is an agent of the partnership for the purpose of its business. An act of a partner, including the execution of an instrument in the partnership name, for apparently carrying on in the ordinary course the partnership business or business of the kind carried on by the partnership binds the partnership, unless the partner had no authority to act for the partnership in the particular matter and the person with whom the partner was dealing knew or had received a notification that the partner lacked authority."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16301(1), Cal. Corp. Code § 16301, subd. (1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16301.)
  "An act of a partner that is not apparently for carrying on in the ordinary course the partnership business or business of the kind carried on by the partnership binds the partnership only if the act was authorized by the other partners."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16301(2), Cal. Corp. Code § 16301, subd. (2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16301.)
  Known gap: This clause states the default agency rule of Corporations Code § 16301 in full; it does not determine, for any particular transaction involving Morgan & Lee Consulting, whether that transaction was or was not apparently within the ordinary course of the partnership's actual business — that is a fact question resolved by the specific business the partnership conducts and the specific transaction at issue, illustrated in this document's companion clause discussing Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng. Both quotes below are subdivisions (1) and (2) of the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

FILING A STATEMENT OF PARTNERSHIP AUTHORITY AND ITS REQUIRED CONTENT
California law permits, but does not require, a partnership to file a statement of partnership authority. If Morgan & Lee Consulting files one, the statement must include the partnership's name; the street address of its principal office and of one principal office in California, if it has one; the mailing address of its principal office, if different; the names and mailing addresses of all the partners, or of an agent appointed and maintained by the partnership for the purpose of maintaining that list; and the names of the partners authorized to execute an instrument transferring real property held in the partnership's name. Beyond that required content, the statement may also specify the authority, or limitations on the authority, of some or all of Morgan & Lee Consulting's partners to enter into other transactions on the partnership's behalf, and any other matter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A partnership may file a statement of partnership authority, which is subject to all of the following: (1) The statement shall include all of the following: (A) The name of the partnership. (B) The street address of its principal office and of one principal office in California, if there is one. (C) The mailing address of its principal office, if different from the street addresses specified pursuant to subparagraph (B). (D) The names and mailing addresses of all of the partners or of an agent appointed and maintained by the partnership for the purpose of subdivision (b). (E) The names of the partners authorized to execute an instrument transferring real property held in the name of the partnership. (2) The statement may specify the authority, or limitations on the authority, of some or all of the partners to enter into other transactions on behalf of the partnership and any other matter."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(a), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  Known gap: This clause states the filing option and required content of Corporations Code § 16303, subdivision (a); it does not state the statement's legal effect on third parties, which this document's companion clauses on subdivisions (d), (e), and (f) address separately, and it does not state the general execution and filing mechanics that apply to statements under this chapter, covered in this document's companion clause on Corporations Code § 16105.

IF THE STATEMENT NAMES AN AGENT INSTEAD OF LISTING EVERY PARTNER
Rather than listing every partner's name and mailing address directly in the statement, Morgan & Lee Consulting's statement of partnership authority may instead name an agent appointed and maintained by the partnership for that purpose. If it does, the named agent must maintain a list of the names and mailing addresses of all of Morgan & Lee Consulting's partners and make that list available to any person who requests it, on a showing of good cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "If a statement of partnership authority names an agent, the agent shall maintain a list of the names and mailing addresses of all of the partners and make it available to any person on request for good cause shown."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(b), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the agent-list mechanism of Corporations Code § 16303, subdivision (b); it does not define what showing satisfies "good cause" for a request, a term the statute does not itself define, and it does not address the separate statutory role of an agent for service of process, which this project's existing Agent for Service of Process — Duties and Change of Agent Information Sheet covers as a distinct filing requirement.

LEGAL EFFECT ON THIRD PARTIES: A FILED GRANT OF AUTHORITY CAN BECOME CONCLUSIVE
A filed statement of partnership authority does more than provide information — it can supplement a partner's actual authority to act for Morgan & Lee Consulting as to third parties. Except for real property transfers, a grant of authority contained in a filed statement is conclusive in favor of a person who gives value without knowledge to the contrary, so long as no limitation on that authority is then contained in another filed statement; if a filed cancellation later removes such a limitation, the previous grant of authority revives. A separate, parallel rule governs transfers of real property held in Morgan & Lee Consulting's name: a grant of authority to transfer that real property, contained in a certified copy of a filed statement that has been recorded in the office for recording transfers of that real property, is similarly conclusive in favor of a person who gives value without knowledge to the contrary, so long as no recorded certified copy of a filed statement containing a limitation on that authority is then of record; recording a certified copy of a filed cancellation of such a limitation likewise revives the previous grant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Except for transfers of real property, a grant of authority contained in a filed statement of partnership authority is conclusive in favor of a person who gives value without knowledge to the contrary, so long as and to the extent that a limitation on that authority is not then contained in another filed statement. A filed cancellation of a limitation on authority revives the previous grant of authority."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(d)(1), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  "A grant of authority to transfer real property held in the name of the partnership contained in a certified copy of a filed statement of partnership authority recorded in the office for recording transfers of that real property is conclusive in favor of a person who gives value without knowledge to the contrary, so long as and to the extent that a certified copy of a filed statement containing a limitation on that authority is not then of record in the office for recording transfers of that real property. The recording in the office for recording transfers of that real property of a certified copy of a filed cancellation of a limitation on authority revives the previous grant of authority."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(d)(2), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  Known gap: This clause states the conclusive-grant-of-authority rules of Corporations Code § 16303, subdivision (d), paragraphs (1) and (2); it does not determine, for any specific transaction, whether a specific person in fact "gave value without knowledge to the contrary" — a fact question this sheet does not resolve. It also does not address the separate, narrower notice rules that apply to limitations rather than grants of authority, covered in this document's companion clause on subdivisions (e) and (f) of the same section.

NOTICE OF LIMITATIONS ON AUTHORITY: RECORDED REAL PROPERTY LIMITS ARE DIFFERENT FROM EVERYTHING ELSE
California law treats a limitation on a partner's authority differently depending on whether it concerns real property and whether it has been recorded. A person who is not a partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting is deemed to know of a limitation on a partner's authority to transfer real property held in the partnership's name only if a certified copy of the filed statement containing that limitation is of record in the office for recording transfers of that real property. Outside of that specific recorded-real-property circumstance — and outside a small number of other statutory exceptions — a person who is not a partner is not deemed to know of a limitation on a partner's authority merely because the limitation is contained in a filed statement at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A person not a partner is deemed to know of a limitation on the authority of a partner to transfer real property held in the name of the partnership if a certified copy of the filed statement containing the limitation on authority is of record in the office for recording transfers of that real property."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(e), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (d) and (e) and Sections 16704 and 16805, a person not a partner is not deemed to know of a limitation on the authority of a partner merely because the limitation is contained in a filed statement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16303(f), Cal. Corp. Code § 16303, subd. (f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16303.)
  Known gap: This clause states the constructive-notice rules of Corporations Code § 16303, subdivisions (e) and (f); the exceptions subdivision (f) itself cross-references — Corporations Code §§ 16704 and 16805 — govern notice in the specific contexts of a dissociated partner's continuing apparent authority and of winding up a dissolved partnership, respectively, and are not restated or analyzed here. This clause does not determine whether any specific person had actual or constructive knowledge of any specific limitation on any specific partner's authority.

THE STATEMENT OF DENIAL: HOW A NAMED PARTNER CAN CONTEST THE FILING
A person named as a partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting — either in a filed statement of partnership authority or in a partner list an agent maintains under that statement — may file a statement of denial. A statement of denial states the partnership's name as filed with the Secretary of State, any identification number the Secretary of State has issued, and the fact being denied, which can include denying a person's authority or denying that the person is a partner at all. Once filed, a statement of denial itself operates as a limitation on authority, governed by the same subdivisions (d) and (e) of section 16303 that govern other filed limitations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A partner or other person named as a partner in a filed statement of partnership authority or in a list maintained by an agent pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 16303 may file a statement of denial stating the name of the partnership as filed with the Secretary of State, any identification number issued by the Secretary of State, and the fact that is being denied, that may include denial of a person’s authority or status as a partner. A statement of denial is a limitation on authority as provided in subdivisions (d) and (e) of Section 16303."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16304, Cal. Corp. Code § 16304 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16304.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statement-of-denial mechanism of Corporations Code § 16304 in full. It does not address the separate, narrower right of a general partner in a California limited partnership to contest authority (a limited partnership is governed by a different statutory chapter, addressed in this project's existing California Limited Partnership Formation — Information Sheet), and it does not determine whether any specific denial made under this section is factually accurate.

FILING MECHANICS: EXECUTION, AMENDMENT, CANCELLATION, AND NOTICE TO PARTNERS
General filing mechanics in the same chapter apply to any statement filed under this chapter, including a statement of partnership authority. A statement is filed in the office of the Secretary of State; a certified copy of a statement already filed in another state's corresponding office may also be filed there, and either filing carries the effect this chapter provides as to partnership property located in, or transactions occurring in, California. A statement filed on Morgan & Lee Consulting's behalf must be executed by at least two partners, and the individual who executes a statement as, or on behalf of, a partner or other person named as a partner must personally declare under penalty of perjury that its contents are accurate. A person authorized to file a statement may later amend or cancel it by filing an amendment or cancellation naming the partnership, identifying the statement, and stating the substance of the change. Whoever files a statement must promptly send a copy to every nonfiling partner and to any other person named as a partner in it — though failing to do so does not limit the statement's effectiveness as to a person who is not a partner. The Secretary of State may charge a fee to file or certify a copy of a statement, and the real-property recording officer may separately charge a fee to record one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "A statement may be filed in the office of the Secretary of State. A certified copy of a statement that is filed in an office in another state may be filed in the office of the Secretary of State. Either filing has the effect provided in this chapter with respect to partnership property located in or transactions that occur in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16105(a), Cal. Corp. Code § 16105, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16105.)
  "A statement filed by a partnership shall be executed by at least two partners. Other statements shall be executed by a partner or other person authorized by this chapter. An individual who executes a statement as, or on behalf of, a partner or other person named as a partner in a statement shall personally declare under penalty of perjury that the contents of the statement are accurate."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16105(c), Cal. Corp. Code § 16105, subd. (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16105.)
  "A person authorized by this chapter to file a statement may amend or cancel the statement by filing an amendment or cancellation that names the partnership, identifies the statement, and states the substance of the amendment or cancellation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16105(d), Cal. Corp. Code § 16105, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16105.)
  "A person who files a statement pursuant to this section shall promptly send a copy of the statement to every nonfiling partner and to any other person named as a partner in the statement. Failure to send a copy of a statement to a partner or other person does not limit the effectiveness of the statement as to a person not a partner."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16105(e), Cal. Corp. Code § 16105, subd. (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16105.)
  "The Secretary of State may collect a fee for filing or providing a certified copy of a statement. The officer responsible for recording transfers of real property may collect a fee for recording a statement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16105(f), Cal. Corp. Code § 16105, subd. (f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16105.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general filing, execution, amendment, notice, and fee mechanics of Corporations Code § 16105, subdivisions (a) through (f); it does not restate subdivision (g)'s separate procedure for the Secretary of State to cancel a statement after a dishonored filing-fee payment, which is a narrower contingency not addressed here. It does not state the dollar amount of any filing or recording fee, which the statute leaves to be set elsewhere rather than fixing in this section's text, and it does not address the recording office's own separately-set recording fee schedule.

HOW PARTNERSHIP PROPERTY IS TRANSFERRED DEPENDS ON HOW TITLE IS HELD
The statement-of-partnership-authority rules connect directly to how Morgan & Lee Consulting's property can be transferred, because the transfer mechanics themselves turn on how title to that property is held. Subject to the effect of any filed statement of partnership authority, property held in the partnership's own name may be transferred by an instrument a partner executes in the partnership's name. Property held instead in the name of one or more partners, where the instrument that transferred it to them indicated their capacity as partners or the existence of a partnership (without naming the partnership itself), may be transferred by an instrument the record titleholders execute. And property held in the name of one or more persons other than the partnership, with no such indication of partnership capacity at all, may likewise be transferred by an instrument the record titleholders execute. The statute also allows the partnership to recover property from certain transferees under specified conditions, and provides that if one person comes to hold all of the partners' interests, the partnership property vests in that person, who may then execute and file or record a document evidencing that vesting.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Partnership property may be transferred as follows: (1) Subject to the effect of a statement of partnership authority under Section 16303, partnership property held in the name of the partnership may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by a partner in the partnership name. (2) Partnership property held in the name of one or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring the property to them of their capacity as partners or of the existence of a partnership, but without an indication of the name of the partnership, may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by the persons in whose name the property is held. (3) Partnership property held in the name of one or more persons other than the partnership, without an indication in the instrument transferring the property to them of their capacity as partners or of the existence of a partnership, may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by the persons in whose name the property is held."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16302(a), Cal. Corp. Code § 16302, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16302.)
  "If a person holds all of the partners’ interests in the partnership, all of the partnership property vests in that person. The person may execute a document in the name of the partnership to evidence vesting of the property in that person and may file or record the document."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 16302(d), Cal. Corp. Code § 16302, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=16302.)
  Known gap: This clause states the property-transfer-by-holding-form rules of Corporations Code § 16302, subdivisions (a) and (d); it summarizes rather than quotes verbatim the partnership's more conditional recovery rights against a transferee under subdivisions (b) and (c), which depend on proof of the transferee's actual knowledge or notification and are not restated here in full. It does not determine how title to any specific asset of Morgan & Lee Consulting is currently held or which of these transfer mechanics would apply to it.

HOW COURTS HAVE APPLIED THE ORDINARY-COURSE DISTINCTION: ELIAS REAL ESTATE, LLC V. TSENG
A California Court of Appeal decision illustrates how the ordinary-course distinction in section 16301 actually gets applied to a real transaction. In Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng, four brothers who together operated a clothing import and distribution business also co-owned, as partners, a piece of commercial real property used in that business. One brother signed an agreement to sell the property without the others' written consent, and the buyer sued for specific performance, arguing the sale bound the partnership without a writing because it fell within the selling brother's ordinary authority. The Court of Appeal held that because the partnership's actual business was importing and distributing clothing — not holding or selling real estate — the sale of the property was outside the ordinary course of that business, so it fell under section 16301's second, narrower rule requiring the other partners' actual authorization, and the separate statute of frauds required that authorization to be in writing. The court contrasted this with an earlier case in which a partnership organized specifically to hold and resell unimproved land was found to be acting in the ordinary course when one partner sold the partnership's land, because selling land was that partnership's actual business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "the sale of real property was an act outside the ordinary course of the partnership’s clothing business. Consequently, under section 16301, Arthur’s authority to sell the Property on behalf of his absent brothers had to be in writing."
  — Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng, 156 Cal.App.4th 425 (2007) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2290594/elias-real-estate-llc-v-tseng/)
  "acts of a partner falling under former section 15009, subdivision (1) are not subject to the statute of frauds, while acts falling under subdivision (2) are."
  — Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng, 156 Cal.App.4th 425 (2007) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2290594/elias-real-estate-llc-v-tseng/)
  Known gap: This is one Court of Appeal's application of the ordinary-course distinction to one set of facts — a partnership whose actual business (importing and distributing clothing) did not include buying or selling the real estate it happened to hold — not a general rule about how any partnership's real property sales will be characterized. Whether a specific transaction by a specific partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting is within the partnership's ordinary course depends on Morgan & Lee Consulting's own actual business and the specific transaction, neither of which this sheet evaluates. The case discusses the statute of frauds (Civ. Code § 1624) as a separate, additional writing requirement for real property sale contracts specifically — a requirement independent of, and not addressed in detail by, the statement-of-partnership-authority statutes this document otherwise covers.

CLOSING AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — STATEMENT OF PARTNERSHIP AUTHORITY INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet was prepared for Morgan & Lee Consulting by Jordan T. Reyes on September 9, 2026 in San Diego, California. It reflects the statutory text of Corporations Code §§ 16105, 16301, 16302, 16303, and 16304 as of the date checked above and does not reflect any review of whether Morgan & Lee Consulting has filed, or should file, a statement of partnership authority, a statement of denial, or any amendment or cancellation of either.

Jordan T. Reyes
Date: September 9, 2026
San Diego, California

It also does not address the separate, narrower notice rules that apply to limitations rather than grants of authority, covered in this document's companion clause on subdivisions (e) and (f) of the same section.

expectedJSON.body: California law treats a limitation on a partner's authority differently depending on whether it concerns real property and whether it has been recorded. A person who is not a partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting is deemed to know of a limitation on a partner's authority to transfer real property held in the partnership's name only if a certified copy of the filed statement containing that limitation is of record in the office for recording transfers of that real property. Outside of that specific recorded-real-property circumstance — and outside a small number of other statutory exceptions — a person who is not a partner is not deemed to know of a limitation on a partner's authority merely because the limitation is contained in a filed statement at all.

citations.quote: A person not a partner is deemed to know of a limitation on the authority of a partner to transfer real property held in the name of the partnership if a certified copy of the filed statement containing the limitation on authority is of record in the office for recording transfers of that real property.

Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (d) and (e) and Sections 16704 and 16805, a person not a partner is not deemed to know of a limitation on the authority of a partner merely because the limitation is contained in a filed statement.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the constructive-notice rules of Corporations Code § 16303, subdivisions (e) and (f); the exceptions subdivision (f) itself cross-references — Corporations Code §§ 16704 and 16805 — govern notice in the specific contexts of a dissociated partner's continuing apparent authority and of winding up a dissolved partnership, respectively, and are not restated or analyzed here. This clause does not determine whether any specific person had actual or constructive knowledge of any specific limitation on any specific partner's authority.

expectedJSON.body: A person named as a partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting — either in a filed statement of partnership authority or in a partner list an agent maintains under that statement — may file a statement of denial. A statement of denial states the partnership's name as filed with the Secretary of State, any identification number the Secretary of State has issued, and the fact being denied, which can include denying a person's authority or denying that the person is a partner at all. Once filed, a statement of denial itself operates as a limitation on authority, governed by the same subdivisions (d) and (e) of section 16303 that govern other filed limitations.

citations.quote: A partner or other person named as a partner in a filed statement of partnership authority or in a list maintained by an agent pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 16303 may file a statement of denial stating the name of the partnership as filed with the Secretary of State, any identification number issued by the Secretary of State, and the fact that is being denied, that may include denial of a person’s authority or status as a partner. A statement of denial is a limitation on authority as provided in subdivisions (d) and (e) of Section 16303.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the statement-of-denial mechanism of Corporations Code § 16304 in full. It does not address the separate, narrower right of a general partner in a California limited partnership to contest authority (a limited partnership is governed by a different statutory chapter, addressed in this project's existing California Limited Partnership Formation — Information Sheet), and it does not determine whether any specific denial made under this section is factually accurate.

expectedJSON.body: General filing mechanics in the same chapter apply to any statement filed under this chapter, including a statement of partnership authority. A statement is filed in the office of the Secretary of State; a certified copy of a statement already filed in another state's corresponding office may also be filed there, and either filing carries the effect this chapter provides as to partnership property located in, or transactions occurring in, California. A statement filed on Morgan & Lee Consulting's behalf must be executed by at least two partners, and the individual who executes a statement as, or on behalf of, a partner or other person named as a partner must personally declare under penalty of perjury that its contents are accurate. A person authorized to file a statement may later amend or cancel it by filing an amendment or cancellation naming the partnership, identifying the statement, and stating the substance of the change. Whoever files a statement must promptly send a copy to every nonfiling partner and to any other person named as a partner in it — though failing to do so does not limit the statement's effectiveness as to a person who is not a partner. The Secretary of State may charge a fee to file or certify a copy of a statement, and the real-property recording officer may separately charge a fee to record one.

citations.quote: A statement may be filed in the office of the Secretary of State. A certified copy of a statement that is filed in an office in another state may be filed in the office of the Secretary of State. Either filing has the effect provided in this chapter with respect to partnership property located in or transactions that occur in this state.

A statement filed by a partnership shall be executed by at least two partners. Other statements shall be executed by a partner or other person authorized by this chapter. An individual who executes a statement as, or on behalf of, a partner or other person named as a partner in a statement shall personally declare under penalty of perjury that the contents of the statement are accurate.

A person authorized by this chapter to file a statement may amend or cancel the statement by filing an amendment or cancellation that names the partnership, identifies the statement, and states the substance of the amendment or cancellation.

A person who files a statement pursuant to this section shall promptly send a copy of the statement to every nonfiling partner and to any other person named as a partner in the statement. Failure to send a copy of a statement to a partner or other person does not limit the effectiveness of the statement as to a person not a partner.

The Secretary of State may collect a fee for filing or providing a certified copy of a statement. The officer responsible for recording transfers of real property may collect a fee for recording a statement.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general filing, execution, amendment, notice, and fee mechanics of Corporations Code § 16105, subdivisions (a) through (f); it does not restate subdivision (g)'s separate procedure for the Secretary of State to cancel a statement after a dishonored filing-fee payment, which is a narrower contingency not addressed here. It does not state the dollar amount of any filing or recording fee, which the statute leaves to be set elsewhere rather than fixing in this section's text, and it does not address the recording office's own separately-set recording fee schedule.

expectedJSON.body: The statement-of-partnership-authority rules connect directly to how Morgan & Lee Consulting's property can be transferred, because the transfer mechanics themselves turn on how title to that property is held. Subject to the effect of any filed statement of partnership authority, property held in the partnership's own name may be transferred by an instrument a partner executes in the partnership's name. Property held instead in the name of one or more partners, where the instrument that transferred it to them indicated their capacity as partners or the existence of a partnership (without naming the partnership itself), may be transferred by an instrument the record titleholders execute. And property held in the name of one or more persons other than the partnership, with no such indication of partnership capacity at all, may likewise be transferred by an instrument the record titleholders execute. The statute also allows the partnership to recover property from certain transferees under specified conditions, and provides that if one person comes to hold all of the partners' interests, the partnership property vests in that person, who may then execute and file or record a document evidencing that vesting.

citations.quote: Partnership property may be transferred as follows: (1) Subject to the effect of a statement of partnership authority under Section 16303, partnership property held in the name of the partnership may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by a partner in the partnership name. (2) Partnership property held in the name of one or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring the property to them of their capacity as partners or of the existence of a partnership, but without an indication of the name of the partnership, may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by the persons in whose name the property is held. (3) Partnership property held in the name of one or more persons other than the partnership, without an indication in the instrument transferring the property to them of their capacity as partners or of the existence of a partnership, may be transferred by an instrument of transfer executed by the persons in whose name the property is held.

If a person holds all of the partners’ interests in the partnership, all of the partnership property vests in that person. The person may execute a document in the name of the partnership to evidence vesting of the property in that person and may file or record the document.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the property-transfer-by-holding-form rules of Corporations Code § 16302, subdivisions (a) and (d); it summarizes rather than quotes verbatim the partnership's more conditional recovery rights against a transferee under subdivisions (b) and (c), which depend on proof of the transferee's actual knowledge or notification and are not restated here in full. It does not determine how title to any specific asset of Morgan & Lee Consulting is currently held or which of these transfer mechanics would apply to it.

expectedJSON.body: A California Court of Appeal decision illustrates how the ordinary-course distinction in section 16301 actually gets applied to a real transaction. In Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng, four brothers who together operated a clothing import and distribution business also co-owned, as partners, a piece of commercial real property used in that business. One brother signed an agreement to sell the property without the others' written consent, and the buyer sued for specific performance, arguing the sale bound the partnership without a writing because it fell within the selling brother's ordinary authority. The Court of Appeal held that because the partnership's actual business was importing and distributing clothing — not holding or selling real estate — the sale of the property was outside the ordinary course of that business, so it fell under section 16301's second, narrower rule requiring the other partners' actual authorization, and the separate statute of frauds required that authorization to be in writing. The court contrasted this with an earlier case in which a partnership organized specifically to hold and resell unimproved land was found to be acting in the ordinary course when one partner sold the partnership's land, because selling land was that partnership's actual business.

citations.case: Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng
citations.quote: the sale of real property was an act outside the ordinary course of the partnership’s clothing business. Consequently, under section 16301, Arthur’s authority to sell the Property on behalf of his absent brothers had to be in writing.

citations.case: Elias Real Estate, LLC v. Tseng
citations.quote: acts of a partner falling under former section 15009, subdivision (1) are not subject to the statute of frauds, while acts falling under subdivision (2) are.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one Court of Appeal's application of the ordinary-course distinction to one set of facts — a partnership whose actual business (importing and distributing clothing) did not include buying or selling the real estate it happened to hold — not a general rule about how any partnership's real property sales will be characterized. Whether a specific transaction by a specific partner of Morgan & Lee Consulting is within the partnership's ordinary course depends on Morgan & Lee Consulting's own actual business and the specific transaction, neither of which this sheet evaluates. The case discusses the statute of frauds (Civ. Code § 1624) as a separate, additional writing requirement for real property sale contracts specifically — a requirement independent of, and not addressed in detail by, the statement-of-partnership-authority statutes this document otherwise covers.
